text: You're given a mountain array — it goes strictly up to a peak, then strictly down. Return the smallest index where the value equals target, or minus one. You can't touch the array directly. You only get get of i, and length.

Thanks. Before I dive in, I'd like to clarify a few things. Just to make sure I'm understanding this correctly — get is the only window I have into the data, so every value I look at costs me something. Is there a cap on how many times I can call it?
Yes. More than a hundred calls and you're judged Wrong Answer. The length is between three and ten to the fourth.

Hmm, that's the real constraint here. The array can hold ten thousand items, and I get a hundred looks — one percent of it. A scan is dead on arrival, and the limit isn't about time at all; it's about how many questions I'm allowed to ask. A hundred is a deliberate number: log base two of ten thousand is about thirteen, so a handful of binary searches fits, and nothing linear does. Two more things to pin down. Strictly up then strictly down means no two neighbors are ever equal — I'll lean on that hard. And the peak is never at either end, right?
Correct on both. The peak index is strictly between zero and length minus one.

Good. On the example, one, two, three, four, five, three, one with target three: the peak is at index four, and three shows up twice — at index two going up, and index five coming down. The answer is two, the smaller one. That gives me a useful fact: each half is strictly monotonic, so no value repeats within a half, and any target appears at most twice — once on each side. I'll use that later.

Hmm, let me think about this for a sec. A naive approach would walk from index zero and stop at the first match. That's guaranteed to give the smallest index, but it costs up to ten to the fourth calls against a budget of a hundred. Out. Binary searching the whole thing in one shot is cheap, but wrong: the array isn't sorted, so when I land below my target I can't tell whether to go left or right — it depends on which slope I'm on. This problem reminds me of splitting at a turning point: the array isn't sorted as a whole, but it's made of two sorted runs. Find the seam, then binary search each run normally. And finding the peak is also a binary search — on the slope, not on the values.

Here's the plan. One: find the peak by comparing mid with mid plus one. Going up, mid can't be the peak, so left becomes mid plus one; going down, mid might be the peak, so I keep it — right equals mid, not mid minus one. Two: binary search the increasing left half, peak included. Three: if that misses, binary search the decreasing right half. One thing worth flagging: searching the left half first alone gives the smallest index — the target appears at most once per side, and every left index is below every right index. That leans on strict monotonicity; with ties I'd need a proper lower-bound search. Phase one reads two cells per round, so the budget is four log n, about fifty-six — not three log n. Does this approach sound good, or would you rather I think of another way?
Sounds good. Let's see the code.

Alright, let me code this up. The main function finds the peak, then calls one helper twice — ascending on the left, descending on the right. One thing worth flagging is the helper's direction test: value less than target, compared for equality with ascending. If the two booleans agree, go right; if they disagree, go left. On a falling run, too small means go left, so this one expression handles both sides. Drop the equals-ascending part and the descending half breaks — on zero, three, two, one looking for one, it returns minus one instead of three. And get of mid plus one is always in range, because the peak loop runs only while left is less than right.

Let's dry-run the code with one, three, five, seven, six, four, two and target four — it misses on the left, so all three phases run. The row that matters is where the peak lands at index three, after six calls: each peak round costs two, because I read mid and mid plus one together. The left half misses in two more calls, and the right half hits index five on call nine. That matches. Corner cases on one, five, two: target five is the peak itself, index one in six calls. Target two hits on the right, index two. Target nine misses both, minus one. And the example with two threes returns index two, since the left is searched first.

Time is log n — three binary searches back to back. Space is constant, just a few index variables. But the number that actually matters here is calls to get: four log n, about fifty-six at the top end. I measured the worst case at ten to the fourth across every peak position and target: fifty-three calls, leaving forty-seven of headroom. No overflow risk — values are only compared, never added, and the midpoint is lo plus half the gap. Oh, one more thing — a hash-map cache only takes the worst case from fifty-three to fifty, so I'd leave it out. And this all rests on strict monotonicity: on zero, zero, one, zero looking for zero, this code returns one when the answer is zero.

Strong. Three things stood out. You read the call limit as the real constraint and worked out what it was designed to allow, before writing anything. You explained why the two peak-finding branches are asymmetric — rising proves mid isn't the peak, falling doesn't — and that's exactly why one gets a plus one and the other doesn't. And you tracked the constant factor, not just the big-O: phase one costs double, and a cache buys back only three calls, so you chose not to ship it. That's real engineering judgment.
